items.title: Mitchel McAllister Interview, 1960-03-19
items.q: And Bud's son, I know he ran away from the band at one time... And, uh, we had, uh, Bud's son was, practically, he was a wizard on saxophone.

ctx.x: Ooh, 78. You've got a right good age, huh? Did they have any trumpets or clarinets or saxophones or trombones when you were young?

No, sir. The first one came in here was the colored fellow by the name of Frank Brakely. He played trombone. Trombone was first. Then the little short cornet. And then people began to add sax. And Bud's son, I know he ran away from the band at one time, and he decided he would, he thought within himself that he would learn to play sax. And he got on his father and warned him to learn him sax. To buy him a sax, at least. And his father gave him a sax. And he was just, he mastered that for just, he wasn't a month.
He was reading a little, and he got to be a perfect wizard on that side.

items.title: Mitchel McAllister Interview, 1960-03-19
items.q: That's what Bud liked, because you had to give it behind him. Maybe then he'd drown you out with his voice.

ctx.x: Oh, I see. Did you ever hear any of the songs the Roustabout sang on the river, loading and unloading? Things like Alberta, let your hair hang old?

I remember that, but who knows who can I. Well, of course, we practiced that. We were all upstairs at all times. And so they're taking us into New Orleans. And we got into the St. Charles Hotel. And they had a heavy orchestra there. And they had us dressed like the old farmers with the big hats and the overalls. And so we went in there. And now, the first had taken us out to the riverfront. We got in there just a little before the big boats got in. And all the big heavy orchestra was cutting up out there in the…
Did you do any country music?
